Commentary of Ibn Juzayy (al-Tashil) on surah 34, verse 1:

﴿Praise belongs to Him in the Hereafter﴾. It is possible that the first praise refers to the world (al-dunya) and the second to the Hereafter (al-akhira), and az-Zamakhshari (rahimahu Allah) understood it this way. But in my view it is also possible that the first praise is meant in its generality and comprehensiveness, so that praise in this world and in the Hereafter is gathered together, and then praise is singled out for the Hereafter, as in His saying: ﴿fruit, and palm trees, and pomegranates﴾ [ar-Rahman: 68]. Then, the praise in the Hereafter may be intended as a genus (al-jins), or it may refer to His saying: ﴿And the last of their call will be: "All praise is due to Allah, Lord of the worlds"﴾ [Yunus: 10], or to His saying: ﴿"All praise is due to Allah, who has fulfilled His promise to us"﴾ [az-Zumar: 74].

﴿What enters into the earth﴾, that is, what goes into it of rain, of the dead, and other things; ﴿and what comes out of it﴾, of plants and other things; ﴿and what descends from the sky﴾, of rain, angels, mercy, punishment, and other things; ﴿and what ascends into it﴾, that is, what rises and climbs up of deeds and other things.

Commentary of Ibn Juzayy (al-Tashil) on surah 34, verses 3–4:

﴿And those who disbelieve say: "The Hour will not come upon us."﴾ It is narrated that the one who uttered this statement was Abu Sufyan ibn Harb. ﴿Not an atom's weight escapes Him﴾, meaning: it does not go absent or remain hidden. ﴿Nor is there anything smaller than that or greater﴾ is conjoined (ma'tuf) to "atom's weight" (mithqal). Al-Zamakhshari said: it is a subject (mubtada'), because the particle of exception (illa, lit. "except") is among the particles of conjunction, and there is no disagreement among the Seven Readers (al-qurra' al-sab'a) on the nominative (raf') of "smaller" (asghar) and "greater" (akbar) in this place. Ibn 'Atiyya did relate a disagreement on it from some of the Seven Readers, but the disagreement concerns [the verse in] Yunus [61]. ﴿In a clear Book﴾, meaning the Preserved Tablet (al-lawh al-mahfuz). ﴿That He may reward﴾ is related (muta'allaq) either to His saying ﴿most surely it will come to you﴾, or to His saying ﴿does not escape﴾, or it is in the sense of His saying ﴿in a clear Book﴾.

Commentary of Ibn Juzayy (al-Tashil) on surah 34, verses 3–4:

﴿And those who disbelieve say: "The Hour will not come upon us."﴾ It is narrated that the one who uttered this statement was Abu Sufyan ibn Harb. ﴿Not an atom's weight escapes Him﴾, meaning: it does not go absent or remain hidden. ﴿Nor is there anything smaller than that or greater﴾ is conjoined (ma'tuf) to "atom's weight" (mithqal). Al-Zamakhshari said: it is a subject (mubtada'), because the particle of exception (illa, lit. "except") is among the particles of conjunction, and there is no disagreement among the Seven Readers (al-qurra' al-sab'a) on the nominative (raf') of "smaller" (asghar) and "greater" (akbar) in this place. Ibn 'Atiyya did relate a disagreement on it from some of the Seven Readers, but the disagreement concerns [the verse in] Yunus [61]. ﴿In a clear Book﴾, meaning the Preserved Tablet (al-lawh al-mahfuz). ﴿That He may reward﴾ is related (muta'allaq) either to His saying ﴿most surely it will come to you﴾, or to His saying ﴿does not escape﴾, or it is in the sense of His saying ﴿in a clear Book﴾.

﴿وَٱلَّذِينَ سَعَوْا﴾ (And those who strived): the subject (mubtada') of the sentence, and its predicate (khabar) is the clause that follows it. Ibn 'Atiyyah said: it is conjoined (ma'tuf) to the first "alladhina" (those). The meaning of "sa'aw" has been mentioned in al-Hajj [51]. As for "mu'ajizin" (those who try to thwart), and "alim" (painful): with the nominative (raf') vowel, it is the recitation of Hafs, as an attribute (sifah) of "adhab" (punishment); with the genitive (khafd) vowel, it is the recitation of Nafi' and others, as an attribute of "rijz" (torment).

﴿And sees﴾ is conjoined (*ma'tuf*, grammatically linked) to ﴿so that He may recompense﴾, or it is a new independent sentence (*mustaʾnaf*, resumptive). This second reading is more apparent. ﴿Those who have been given knowledge﴾ are the Companions, or those from the People of the Book who embraced Islam, or the term is general. ﴿The truth﴾ is the second object (*maf'ul thani*) of ﴿sees﴾, because the seeing here is of the heart, in the sense of knowing. The pronoun is a separator pronoun (*damir fasl*, a pronoun that marks the boundary between the two objects).

Commentary of Ibn Juzayy (al-Tashil) on surah 34, verse 7:

﴿وَقَالَ ٱلَّذِينَ كَفَرُواْ﴾ That is, some of them said to others: ﴿Shall we direct you to a man (meaning Muhammad ﷺ) who will inform you that when you are completely torn apart, ﴿you will be in a new creation﴾?﴾ The meaning of ﴿مُزِّقْتُمْ﴾ (muzziqtum, "torn apart") is: you decay in the graves and your joints are scattered. ﴿كُلَّ مُمَزَّقٍ﴾ (kulla mumazzaq, "every tearing apart") is a verbal noun (maṣdar). The "new creation" is the gathering (ḥashr) on the Day of Resurrection. The governing element (ʿāmil) of ﴿إِذَا﴾ (idha, "when") is the meaning of ﴿إِنَّكُمْ لَفِي خَلْقٍ جَدِيدٍ﴾, because its meaning is: you will be resurrected when you are torn apart. It has been said that the governing element is a hidden verb supposed to precede it, but that is weak. ﴿إِنَّكُمْ لَفِي خَلْقٍ جَدِيدٍ﴾ is the object of ﴿يُنَبِّئُكُمْ﴾ (yunabbi'ukum, "informs you"), and the lam in its predicate was given a kasra (the lam of the predicate is pronounced with a kasra, i.e., it is read as ﴿لِفِي﴾ in the sense of the lam of emphasis being marked). The meaning of the verse is that this man informs you that you will be resurrected after you have decayed in the earth, and their intention was to deem the gathering (ḥashr) unlikely.

Ibn Juzayy (al-Tashil) on surah 34, verse 8:

﴿Has he invented a lie against Allah?﴾ This is part of the speech of the disbelievers. The interrogative hamzah (hamzat al-istifham) was placed before the alif of connection (alif al-wasl), so the alif of connection was dropped and the hamzah remained, vowelled with a fatha and not elongated (ghayr mamdudah). ﴿Rather, those who do not believe in the Hereafter are in the punishment﴾ This is a refutation of them: that is, he has not invented a lie against Allah, and there is no madness in him; rather, these disbelievers are in misguidance and confusion away from the truth, which brings them punishment. It may be that by the punishment he means the punishment of the Hereafter, or the punishment in this world through their opposition to the truth and their attempts to make falsehood prevail.

The pronoun in "yarau" (they see) refers to the disbelievers who deny the Resurrection. The heaven and the earth are described as being "before them and behind them" because they encompass them. The meaning is: have they not looked at the heaven and the earth, so that they would know that He who created them is able to resurrect people after their death? It is also possible that the meaning is a threat to them, which is then explained by His words: ﴿If We wish, We shall cause the earth to swallow them, or We shall make a piece of the heaven fall upon them﴾. That is: have they not seen the heaven and the earth, that they encompass them, so that they would know that they have no escape from God? ﴿Indeed in that is a sign﴾. The reference is either to the heaven's encompassing of them, or to the greatness of the heaven and the earth, in that they contain a sign indicating the Resurrection.

Commentary of Ibn Juzayy (al-Tashil) on surah 34, verse 10:

﴿O mountains, echo the glorification with him﴾. Its implied sense is: "We said, O mountains." The clause is an explanation of "fadlan" (grace). The meaning of "awwibi" is "glorify," and its origin is from "ta'wib," which is "tarjî" (repetition, returning the melody). It is as if he repeated the glorification and they repeated it with him. It was also said: it derives from "ta'wib" in the sense of traveling by day. And it was said: he would wail, and the mountains would respond to him with their echoes, and the birds with their calls. ﴿And the birds﴾ is in the accusative, a conjunction with the place of "O mountains." It was also said that it is a direct object in the sense of "with" (maf'ul ma'ah). It was also said that it is conjoined to "fadlan." It is also read in the nominative, as a conjunction with the wording of "O mountains." ﴿And We made iron soft for him﴾, that is, We made it pliable for him without fire, like clay and dough. It was also said: because iron was his, owing to the intensity of his strength.

﴿Full coats of mail﴾ are the armour that covers the body. ﴿And measure well in the weaving﴾. The meaning of *al-sard* (the weaving or linking of rings in mail) here is the weaving of armour. Its measure is that the ring should be neither so small that it becomes weak, nor so large that the one wearing it is struck through its gaps. It is also said: the rivet should be neither thin nor thick. ﴿And work righteousness﴾ is addressed to Dawud and his family.

And for Solomon, the wind (﴿وَلِسُلَيْمَانَ ٱلرِّيحَ﴾) — read in the accusative on the presumption of "and We subjected," and it was recited in the nominative according to the transmission of Abu Bakr from ʿAsim, as a nominative of inception. ﴿Its morning course was a month, and its evening course was a month﴾: that is, it would carry him in the morning a distance of a month's journey, and in the evening a distance of a month's journey. He would sit upon his throne, which was of wood, and it would carry in it — it is related — four thousand horsemen. The wind would lift it and then carry it. ﴿And We caused a font of copper to flow for him﴾. Ibn ʿAbbas said: a font of copper would flow for him in Yemen, from which he would make whatever he wished. Al-qitr means copper. It was also said: al-qitr is iron, copper, and what is similar to these; four fonts would flow for him from it. It was also said: the meaning is that God melted the copper for him without fire, just as He did with iron for Dawud. ﴿We will make him taste the punishment of the Blaze﴾: meaning the Fire of the Hereafter. It was also said: there was an angel with him who would strike them with a whip of fire.

**﴿Maḥārīb﴾** means palaces; it is also said to mean prayer niches (masājid). **Tamāthīl** (statues): it is said that they were not in the form of living beings, and it is also said that they were in the form of living beings, and that this was permissible among them. **﴿Ka-l-jawāb﴾**: plural of *jābiyah* (a large basin or cistern in which water gathers). **﴿Rāsiyāt﴾**: meaning firmly fixed in their places because of their size. **﴿Iʿmalū Āla Dāwūd shukran﴾**: a narration of what was said to the family of Dawud. *Shukran* is in the accusative, and it may be a *mafʿūl li-ajlih* (object of purpose), or a verbal noun in the position of a circumstantial qualifier (ḥāl), its sense being "thankful," or a verbal noun derived from the meaning, since the action is itself thanks, its sense being "give thanks with thanks," or a direct object (*mafʿūl bih*). **﴿Wa-qalīlun min ʿibādiya al-shakūr﴾**: this may be an address to the family of Dawud, or an address to Muhammad (ﷺ).

Commentary of Ibn Juzayy (al-Tashil) on surah 34, verse 14:

﴿دَابَّةُ الأَرْضِ تَأْكُلُ مِنسَأَتَهُ﴾ [Dābbat al-arḍ taʾkulu minsaʾatahu] "The creature of the earth was eating away at his staff." Al-minsaʾah is the staff (ʿaṣā). It has been read with a hamza and without a hamza. Dābbat al-arḍ is the termite (al-arḍah), the woodworm (al-sūsah) that eats wood and other things. The story behind the verse is that Sulayman, peace be upon him, entered a dome of glass and stood praying, leaning on his staff. His soul was taken while he was leaning on it, and he remained so for a year, with no one knowing of his death, until the staff fell and he toppled to the ground. We have abridged much of what people have mentioned about this story, because it is not sound.

﴿تَبَيَّنَتِ ٱلْجِنُّ﴾ [Tabayyanat al-jinn] "The jinn became clear" — from tabayyana al-shayʾ, meaning it became manifest when it appeared. What follows it is a substitute (badal) for "al-jinn." The meaning is that it became manifest to people that the jinn do not know the unseen. It has also been said that tabayyana here means "knew" (ʿalima), and in that case "that" (anna) and what follows it is the direct object. The meaning would then be: the jinn knew that they do not know the unseen, and they verified that this was after the matter had been obscured to them. Or: the jinn knew that their disbelievers do not know the unseen, and that they (the disbelievers) were lying in their claim to that.

﴿فِي ٱلْعَذَابِ ٱلْمُهِينِ﴾ [Fī al-ʿadhāb al-muhīn] "In the humiliating punishment." It means the service they used to render to Sulayman and his subjugation of them in various kinds of work. The meaning is: had the jinn known the unseen, the death of Sulayman would not have remained hidden from them.

Commentary of Ibn Juzayy (al-Tashil) on surah 34, verse 15:

﴿Indeed there was for Sheba in their dwelling a sign﴾ Sheba (Saba'): a tribe of the Arabs, named after their forefather from whom they descended. It is said that it is named after their mother, and it is said that it is named after their place. The first is the most well-known, because it has been reported in a hadith. Their dwellings were between Syria (al-Sham) and Yemen. ﴿Two gardens on the right and on the left﴾ They had a valley, and the two gardens were on its right and its left. "Two gardens" is either a substitute (badal) for "a sign," or the subject (mubtada') of a sentence, or the predicate (khabar) of an omitted subject. ﴿Eat﴾ Its implied meaning: it was said to them, "Eat from the provision of your Lord." The prophets said this to them, and it is related that thirteen prophets were sent to them, and they denied them. ﴿A good land﴾ That is, abundant in provisions, of good air, and free from vermin.

﴿But they turned away﴾: that is, they turned away from giving thanks to God, or from obeying the prophets. ﴿So We sent upon them the flood of al-ʿArim﴾. They had a dam (sadd) that held back water so that it would rise, and both gardens were irrigated by it. God sent a juradh (juradh, a small creature) against the dam, and it ruined it, so the two gardens dried up. It was also said: when the dam was destroyed, the flood carried away the two gardens and many people. There is disagreement about the meaning of al-ʿArim. It was said that it is al-sadah (a kind of rock or hard ground), and it was said that it is the name of that very valley. It was said that it means "the severe," so that it is an attribute of the flood, from ʿarāma (violence, fierceness). It was said that it is the juradh that ruined the dam, and it was said: a heavy rain. ﴿Of bitter fruit, tamarisk, and a few lote-trees﴾. The word ukul (أكل), with the hamza vowelled with a ḍammah, means "that which is eaten" (al-maʾkūl). Khamṭ (خمط) is the arak tree (Salvadora persica), and it was said: every tree that has thorns. Athl (أثل) is a tree resembling the tamarisk (ṭarfāʾ). Sidr (سدر) is a well-known tree (the lote-tree). The i'rab (إعراب, grammatical analysis) of khamṭ is that it is either a badal (بدل, substitute apposition) for ukul, or an ʿaṭf bayān (عطف بيان, explicative apposition). It was also read in the idafah (إضافة, construct form) [i.e., ukuli khamṭ]. Athl is coordinated (ʿaṭf) with al-ukul, not with khamṭ, because athl has no fruit to eat. The meaning is that when the two gardens mentioned were destroyed, it was said: God replaced them for them with two gardens, the opposite of their description in beauty and provision.

Ibn Juzayy's commentary (al-Tashil) on Surah 34, verse 17:

﴿And do We requite [any] but the ungrateful?﴾ Its meaning: none is called to account and recompensed in kind for his deeds except the disbeliever (al-kafur); for the believer, Allah may grant him leniency and overlook [his sins] for him.

Commentary of Ibn Juzayy (al-Tashil) on surah 34, verse 18:

﴿And We placed between them and the towns which We had blessed visible towns﴾ This verse and what follows describe the condition of Sheba before the coming of the flood and the destruction of their gardens. By "the towns which We had blessed" is meant al-Sham (Greater Syria). "Visible towns" refers to towns connected to one another from their lands up to al-Sham. The meaning of "visible" is that some of them are visible from others because of their proximity. It was also said: they were elevated on hills. Ibn 'Atiyya said: they were outside the cities, as one says "bi-zahir al-madina," meaning outside it. ﴿And We made the travel between them measured﴾ That is, We apportioned the stages of the journey. The towns were contiguous, so the traveler would spend the night in one town and wake up in another, fearing neither hunger nor thirst, needing no provisions to carry, and fearing no one.

Commentary of Ibn Juzayy (al-Tashil) on surah 34, verse 19:

﴿So they said: "Our Lord, make the distances between our journeys far apart."﴾ It was read as ﴿bā'id﴾ (with a short vowel on the ba' and the alif), and Ibn Kathir and Abu 'Amr read ﴿ba''id﴾ (with the 'ayn doubled and shortened in a different form), both in the imperative mood as a request. The meaning is that they became insolent over the blessing and grew weary of well-being, and they asked God to put distance between their closely connected villages so that they could walk through the deserts and prepare provisions for the journeys. So God swiftly answered them. It was also read as ﴿bā'ada﴾ with a fatha on the 'ayn, as a statement, and the meaning then is that they said God had put distance between their villages, and that is a lie and a denial of the blessing. ﴿And they wronged themselves﴾: meaning by their saying ﴿"make the distances between our journeys far apart"﴾, or by their sins in general. ﴿And We made them into scattered fragments﴾: meaning We dispersed them throughout the lands, until their dispersal became a proverb. It is said: "They became the 'dispersed as Saba' (tafarraqu aydi Saba)." And in a hadith: Saba was the father of ten of the tribes; when the flood came upon their lands, they scattered, so six of them went to the right (tayammana) and four went to the left (tashha'ama).

﴿And Iblis had already found his assumption about them to be true﴾. That is, he found his assumption about them to be correct, referring to his words: ﴿I will surely mislead them﴾ [Sad: 82], and his words: ﴿And You will not find most of them grateful﴾ [al-A'raf: 17].

Commentary of Ibn Juzayy (al-Tashil) on Surah 34, verse 22:

﴿Say: Call upon those whom you claimed [to be gods]﴾ is a challenge (ta'jiz) to the polytheists and a establishment of proof against them. By "those whom you claimed" is meant their gods. The object of "you claimed" is omitted, meaning: you claimed that they are gods, or you claimed that they are intercessors. It is reported that this was revealed at the time of the famine that struck the Quraysh. ﴿Of a share﴾ means a portion, and "al-zahir" means the helper.

**Commentary of Ibn Juzayy (al-Tashil) on Surah 34, verse 23:**

﴿And intercession will not benefit with Him except for one whom He has permitted.﴾ The meaning: intercession will not benefit with Allah except for one for whom Allah has permitted that he intercede, for no one intercedes except with His permission. It was also said: the meaning is that intercession will not benefit except for one for whom Allah has permitted that intercession be made on his behalf. The sense is that intercession, in every form, occurs only with the permission of Allah. In this there is a refutation of the polytheists who used to say: "These are our intercessors with Allah." ﴿Until, when fear is removed from their hearts, they say: "What has your Lord said?"﴾ Reports from the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) have been widely transmitted that this verse concerns the angels (peace be upon them). When they hear the revelation sent to Jibril (Gabriel), they are struck with a great terror. When the terror is removed from their hearts, some of them say to others: "What has your Lord said?" They reply: "The Truth." The meaning of ﴿fear is removed from their hearts﴾ is that the fear departs from them. The pronoun in ﴿their hearts﴾ and in ﴿they say﴾ refers to the angels. If it is asked: how is this so, since no earlier mention has been made to which the pronoun could refer? The answer is that there has been an allusion to them in His words ﴿And intercession will not benefit with Him except for one whom He has permitted﴾, because some Arabs used to worship the angels and say: "These are our intercessors with Allah." Mention of intercession necessitates mention of intercessors, so the pronoun refers to the intercessors indicated by the word "intercession." If it is asked: to what does His words ﴿until, when fear is removed from their hearts﴾ connect, and why is "until" (ḥattā) used to indicate a limit (ghāyah)? The answer is that it connects with what is understood from the discourse, namely that there is a waiting for permission, a fear, and a pause, until the fear is removed by the permission to intercede. This is close in meaning to His words: ﴿On the Day when the Spirit and the angels stand in ranks, none will speak except one whom the Most Merciful has permitted﴾ [ʿAmma (An-Naba'): 38]. Some people did not grasp how this verse connects to what precedes it, so they were confused about it, to the point that some of them said: it concerns the disbelievers after death, and the meaning of ﴿fear is removed from their hearts﴾ is that they see the reality, and so it is said to them: ﴿What has your Lord said?﴾ and they reply: "The Truth," and they acknowledge it when acknowledgment no longer benefits them. The correct view, however, is that it concerns the angels, because this is reported in the hadith, and because the purpose is to refute the disbelievers who worshipped the angels; mention of the angels' intense fear of Allah and their exalting of Him is therefore appropriate.

Ibn Juzayy's commentary (al-Tashil) on surah 34, verse 24:

﴿Say: Who provides for you from the heavens and the earth?﴾ This is a question intended to establish the proof against the polytheists. ﴿Say: Allah.﴾ This is an answer to the question with something that cannot be disputed; for this reason the question and the answer came from one side. ﴿And indeed we or you are surely upon guidance or in clear error.﴾ This is a gentle courtesy and a descent in the debate to the utmost degree of fairness, like your saying: "God knows that one of us is upon the truth and the other upon falsehood," without explicitly identifying either of them, but rather alerting the opponent to reflection until he knows who is upon the truth and who is upon falsehood. The purpose of the verse is that the believers are upon guidance and the disbelievers are in clear error.

Ibn Juzayy, *al-Tashil*, on Surah 34, verse 25:

﴿Say: You will not be questioned about what we committed, nor will we be questioned about what you do.﴾ This is a statement that implies conciliation, which was abrogated (*nusikhat*, from *naskh*, abrogation) by the sword.
"Our Lord will bring us together" — literally, ﴿يَفْتَحُ بَيْنَنَا﴾ means "He will judge between us," and al-Fattah (the Opener) means the Judge.

Say: "Show me those whom you have joined with Him as partners." This is an establishment of proof against the polytheists. The seeing here is seeing of the heart (ru'yat qalb), so *shurakāʾ* (شركاء) is the third object (*mafʿūl thālith*). The meaning is: show me, by evidence and proof, those whom you consider to be His partners, and how their partnership is established. It has also been said that this is seeing of the eye (ru'yat baṣar), and that *shurakāʾ* is a *ḥāl* (circumstantial qualifier) of the object in ﴿أَلْحَقْتُمْ﴾, as if He had said: where are those you worship besides Him? In His saying ﴿أَرُونِي﴾ there is belittling of the partners and contempt for them, and a challenge to the polytheists to fail. In His saying ﴿كَلَّا﴾ there is a deterrent for them from associating partners. And in describing God as "the Mighty, the Wise" there is a rebuttal to them, that their partners are not like that.

Commentary of Ibn Juzayy (al-Tashil) on surah 34, verse 28:

﴿And We have not sent you except comprehensively to mankind﴾. The meaning is that God sent Muhammad (ﷺ) to all people, and this is one of the distinctions that God granted him over the rest of the prophets. As for the i'rab (grammatical analysis) of ﴿kaffah﴾, it is a circumstantial accusative (hal) from "mankind," placed before it for emphasis. This is what Ibn 'Atiyya said. Al-Zamakhshari said: that is an error, because it is not permissible for the circumstantial accusative to precede the word it qualifies when that word is in the genitive. His interpretation is: "We have not sent you except as a general message to mankind," so that ﴿kaffah﴾ is an adjective of an omitted verbal noun (masdar). Al-Zajjaj said: the meaning is "We sent you gathering mankind together in warning and good tidings," so he made it a circumstantial accusative from the kaf (the pronoun "you"), and the ta' (in kaffah) on this view is for intensification, like the ta' in rawiyah and 'allamah.

Commentary of Ibn Juzayy (al-Tashil) on surah 34, verses 29–30:

﴿Say: "For you is an appointment of a Day"﴾. He means the Day of Resurrection, or the descent of punishment upon them in this world, which is what they asked about in a mocking manner, when they said: ﴿When is this promise?﴾.

Commentary of Ibn Juzayy (al-Tashil) on surah 34, verses 29–30:

﴿Say: "For you is an appointment of a Day"﴾. He means the Day of Resurrection, or the descent of punishment upon them in this world, which is what they asked about in a mocking manner, when they said: ﴿When is this promise?﴾.

﴿Nor in that which is before it﴾: this means the earlier scriptures, such as the Torah (al-Tawrat) and the Gospel (al-Injil). The disbelievers only made this statement when the proof drawn from what is in the Torah, concerning the mention of Muhammad (ﷺ), was established against them. It has also been said that ﴿that which is before it﴾ refers to the Day of Resurrection, but this is an error and the reverse of what is meant, because "that which is before a thing" is what precedes it.

﴿And if you could see﴾: the answer to "law" (if) is omitted, and its implied meaning is: "you would see a grave matter." ﴿when some of them cast back the word to others﴾: that is, they speak and some of them respond to others. ﴿Rather, you were criminals﴾: that is, you disbelieved by your own choice, not by Our command.

﴿Nor in that which is before it﴾: this means the earlier scriptures, such as the Torah (al-Tawrat) and the Gospel (al-Injil). The disbelievers only made this statement when the proof drawn from what is in the Torah, concerning the mention of Muhammad (ﷺ), was established against them. It has also been said that ﴿that which is before it﴾ refers to the Day of Resurrection, but this is an error and the reverse of what is meant, because "that which is before a thing" is what precedes it.

﴿And if you could see﴾: the answer to "law" (if) is omitted, and its implied meaning is: "you would see a grave matter." ﴿when some of them cast back the word to others﴾: that is, they speak and some of them respond to others. ﴿Rather, you were criminals﴾: that is, you disbelieved by your own choice, not by Our command.

Commentary of Ibn Juzayy (al-Tashil) on surah 34, verses 33–34:

﴿Rather, the plotting of the night and the day﴾. The meaning is that the weak (al-mustad'afun) said to the arrogant (al-mustakbirun): "Rather, your plotting against us by night and day was the cause of our disbelief." The grammatical analysis (i'rab) of ﴿مَكْرُ﴾ (makr, "plotting") is that it is a subject (mubtada', the inchoative noun), and its predicate (khabar) is omitted; or it is the predicate of an implied subject. The noun makr is attributed to "the night and the day" in an extended usage (ittisa'). It may be an attribution to the object or to the agent in a figurative sense (majaz), like their saying: "Its day is fasting and its night is standing in prayer," meaning that it is fasted in and prayed in. The attribution indicates the abundance of the plotting and its continuity through the night and the day. If it is asked: why was the waw (and) affixed in the phrase ﴿الَّذِينَ اسْتُضْعِفُوا﴾ (those who were deemed weak) but not in ﴿لِلَّذِينَ اسْتَكْبَرُوا﴾ (to those who were arrogant)? The answer is that the speech of those who were deemed weak had been mentioned before, so their second speech was joined to it by the conjunction, whereas no other speech of those who were arrogant had been mentioned before it to be joined to. ﴿And they concealed the regret﴾, meaning they hid it within themselves. It was also said that they displayed it, and so it is one of the words with opposite meanings (al-adhdad). The pronoun refers to all of the weak and the arrogant. ﴿Its affluent ones﴾, meaning the people of wealth and luxury in this world, who are the ones who hasten to deny the prophets. The purpose of the verse is to console the Prophet (ﷺ) regarding the denial of the chief men of Quraysh toward him.

﴿And they said: "We have more wealth and children"﴾. The pronoun refers either to the Quraysh or to the earlier affluent people (al-mutrafin). They measured the affair of this world by the affair of the Hereafter, and they thought that just as God gave them wealth and children in this world, He would not punish them in the Hereafter.

Commentary of Ibn Juzayy (al-Tashil) on surah 34, verse 36:

﴿Say, "Indeed, my Lord extends provision to whom He wills and restricts it."﴾ A statement that contains a refutation of them: the extending and restricting of provision in this world depends on the will of God. God may widen provision for the disbeliever and for the sinner, and restrict it for the believer and the obedient, and the reverse. So there is no proof in that concerning the matter of the Hereafter.

Zulfa (nearness): a verbal noun meaning closeness, as if He had said: "Your wealth brings you a nearness." ﴿Except for one who believes﴾: this is an exception from the object in "your wealth brings you," and the meaning is that wealth does not bring nearness except to the believer who is righteous and who spends it in the way of God. It is said that the exception is disjunctive (munqati'), but the first view is better. ﴿A recompense of multiplication﴾: meaning the multiplying of good deeds to ten times their like, and more than that.

**Commentary of Ibn Juzayy (al-Tashil) on Surah 34, verse 39:**

﴿He extends the provision﴾ etc. The verse is repeated because the purpose differs. The purpose of the first occurrence is directed at the disbelievers, while the purpose here is to encourage the believers to spend. ﴿Then He will replace it﴾: the replacement (*al-khalf*) may be in wealth or in reward.

Commentary of Ibn Juzayy (al-Tashil) on surah 34, verse 41:

﴿You are our Guardian, not them.﴾ This is a disavowal by the angels that they had any approval of the polytheists worshipping them, though this does not negate that the polytheists did worship them. ﴿Rather, they used to worship the jinn.﴾ Their worship of the jinn was their obedience to them in disbelief and disobedience. It was said: they used to enter into the hollows of the idols and were thus worshipped through the worship of the idols. It is also possible that some people worshipped the jinn, based on His saying: ﴿And they made the jinn partners with Allah﴾ [al-An'am: 100].

Qur'anic quotation: ﴿And We did not give them any scriptures which they could study﴾ — the verse, in its wording.

Ibn Juzayy's commentary, translated:

"﴿And We did not give them any scriptures which they could study﴾ — concerning its meaning there are two aspects. The first: they have no books that confirm the validity of their claims, nor has any warner come to them who testifies to what they have said; so their claims are false, since they have no proof for them. The purpose on this view is a refutation of them. The second: they have no books and no warner has come to them, so they are in need of someone to teach them and warn them; and for this reason God sent Muhammad (ﷺ) to them. The purpose on this view is to establish the prophethood of Muhammad (ﷺ)."

Commentary of Ibn Juzayy (al-Tashil) on surah 34, verse 45:

﴿وَمَا بَلَغُواْ مِعْشَارَ مَآ آتَيْنَاهُمْ﴾ "Al-Mi'shar" (a tenth) is one-tenth, and it was said it is one-tenth of a tenth. The first is more sound. The pronoun in "balaghu" (they reached) refers to the disbelievers of Quraysh, and the pronoun in "ataynahum" (We gave them) refers to the earlier scriptures. That is: these people have not reached one-tenth of what Allah gave the earlier peoples in strength and wealth. It was also said: the pronoun in "balaghu" refers to the earlier peoples, and the pronoun in "ataynahum" refers to Quraysh, meaning: the earlier peoples did not reach one-tenth of what Allah gave these people in proofs and evidences. The first is more sound, and it is similar to His saying: ﴿they were stronger than them in power﴾. ﴿فَكَيْفَ كَانَ نَكِيرِ﴾ That is, "how was My rejection," meaning the punishment of the earlier disbelievers. In this there is a warning to Quraysh.

Commentary of Ibn Juzayy (al-Tashil) on surah 34, verse 46:

﴿Say: "I only advise you of one thing"﴾ meaning, one matter, approximately, for you ﴿that you stand up for Allah﴾. This is the explanation of the one matter. "That you stand up" is either a substitution (badal), an explanatory apposition ('atf bayan), or the predicate of an implied subject (khabar mubtada' mudmar). Its meaning is that you should stand to examine the affair of Muhammad (ﷺ) with a sincere standing for the sake of Allah, the Exalted, free from following desire or inclination. By "standing" here is not meant standing on the two feet; rather, what is meant is taking up the matter and exerting seriousness in it. ﴿in pairs and individually﴾ is a circumstantial phrase (hal) referring to the pronoun in "taqumu" (you stand). The meaning is that you should stand two by two to debate the matter and seek verification, and stand one by one to gather the mind and collect the thought. Then reflect on the affair of Muhammad (ﷺ), so that you will know that there is no madness in your companion, because he came with clear truth; and in addition, his sayings and actions indicate the soundness of his intellect and the firmness of his knowledge, and that he reached a great degree of wisdom. This indicates that he is neither a madman nor one who fabricates against Allah. ﴿There is no madness in your companion﴾ is connected to what precedes it according to the most correct view: that is, reflect and you will know that there is no madness in your companion. It was also said that it is a new independent statement (isti'naf).

Ibn Juzayy (al-Tashil) on surah 34, verse 47:

﴿Say, "Whatever reward I have asked of you, it is yours."﴾ This is like a man saying to his companion: "If I have given you anything, then take it," while he knows that he has not given him anything; rather, he wants to disclaim having given him anything. The meaning here is similar: it is like your saying, "Say: I do not ask you for any reward for it."

Commentary of Ibn Juzayy (al-Tashil) on surah 34, verse 48:

﴿Say: Indeed, my Lord hurls the truth.﴾ Al-qadhf is throwing (al-ramy), and it is used metaphorically for casting (al-ilqa'). So the meaning is: He casts the truth onto His chosen servants, or He hurls falsehood with truth, so that it perishes. ﴿Knower of the unseen⁽ᵃ⁾ things.﴾ It is the predicate of an implied subject (khabar mubtada' mudmar), or a substitute (badal) for the pronoun in ﴿hurls﴾, or a substitute for the subject of inna (ism inna) according to its place (ʿala al-mawdi').

Commentary of Ibn Juzayy (al-Tashil) on surah 34, verses 49–50:

﴿Say, "The truth has come," meaning Islam, ﴿and falsehood neither originates anything nor restores,﴾ falsehood being disbelief. He negated origination and restoration, meaning that it does nothing and has no manifestation; or it is an expression of its departure, as in His saying: ﴿The truth has come and falsehood has vanished﴾ [al-Isra: 81]. It was also said: falsehood is Satan. ﴿Indeed, He is Hearing, Near﴾, meaning His nearness through His knowledge and encompassing.

Commentary of Ibn Juzayy (al-Tashil) on surah 34, verse 51:

﴿And if you could see when they are terrified﴾ — the response to "if" (law) is omitted; its intended sense is: "you would see a tremendous matter." Or, the meaning of ﴿fazi'u﴾ (they were terrified) is: they hastened to flee. The verb is in the past form but carries the sense of the future, and likewise the verbs that follow it. The time of the terror is the Resurrection (al-ba'th). It is also said to be death, and it is also said to be the Day of Badr. ﴿Then there is no escape﴾, meaning they cannot escape God when they flee. ﴿And they will be seized from a near place﴾, meaning from the place of standing (al-mawqif) to the Fire when they are raised, or from the surface of the earth to its interior when they die, or from the land of Badr to the well (al-qalib). What is meant, according to every view, is the speed with which they are seized.

﴿And they will say, "We have believed in it."﴾ That is, they will say this when they are seized. The pronoun in "it" refers either to God Most High, or to the Prophet (ﷺ), or to the Qur'an, or to Islam. ﴿But how can they reach [faith] from a distant place?﴾ *At-tanawush* (التناوش), with a waw (الواو), means reaching for something. However, *at-tanawush* is an easy, near reach for something that is near. It was also recited with the waw hamzated (بهمز الواو), so the meaning may be the same, and the hamzated form would then mean seeking. The meaning of the verse is to express that their reaching their goal is far-fetched. "A distant place" is an expression for the impossibility of what they intend, for they seek what cannot be, or they want to grasp what they cannot attain, namely their return to the world or their benefiting from faith at that time.

﴿And they had already disbelieved in it⦆ The pronoun refers back to what their statement "﴿We believe in it﴾" referred to. ﴿And they hurl [assumptions] about the unseen from a distant place﴾: "yaqdhifun" (they hurl) is a past-tense verb in meaning, conjoined to "kafaru" (they disbelieved). Its meaning is that they cast their conjectures about unseen matters, saying: there is no resurrection, no Paradise, and no Hellfire. And they say about the Messenger, may Allah's blessings and peace be upon him, that he is a sorcerer or a poet. The "distant place" here is an expression for the invalidity of their conjectures and the remoteness of their statements from the truth.

Commentary of Ibn Juzayy (al-Tashil) on surah 34, verse 54:

﴿And a barrier will be placed between them and what they desire﴾. That is, a barrier will be placed between them and entering Paradise. It was also said: a barrier will be placed between them and benefiting from faith at that time. It was also said: a barrier will be placed between them and the delights of the world and returning to it. ﴿As was done with their like before﴾. This refers to the earlier disbelievers, and He called them "their like" because they agreed in their doctrines. The phrase ﴿from before﴾ may be connected to the verb (fa'ala, "was done"), or to ﴿their like﴾ according to the sense of what precedes it. ﴿In disquieting doubt﴾. This is the strongest and most intense kind of doubt, the darkest in its gloom.
